---
title: "Overview"
---

This is an executable course and research monograph on **Agriculture Derivatives & Quantitative Portfolio Management**. It develops the theory, empirical methods, and implementation architecture needed to analyze, trade, and manage agricultural derivative portfolios using futures, options, physical-market information, and explicit risk constraints.

The purpose is to connect higher-education financial theory to the decisions made by a real derivatives portfolio: what is traded, how it is priced and marked, which risks are carried, how evidence is generated, and how a position is sized, monitored, and attributed.

The work follows a disciplined research loop:

1. state the economic mechanism and the tradable object;
2. define the data, units, timing, and observability assumptions;
3. derive the price, P&L, and risk mapping;
4. estimate or calibrate the model without look-ahead;
5. translate the result into a position and portfolio rule;
6. evaluate costs, liquidity, stress scenarios, attribution, and failure modes.

Each topic is developed through three connected layers: formal theory and derivation; agricultural market interpretation; and a tested implementation that makes assumptions visible.

## Status of this edition {.unnumbered}

This is a living monograph and an initial public edition. Notation, derivations, empirical designs, code interfaces, examples, and references are subject to revision; substantial revisions should be expected as the framework and the research record develop. Published results will be labelled as deterministic fixtures, descriptive statistics, estimated relationships with uncertainty, or simulated/backtested results. These categories are not interchangeable.

## Theory first, applications second {.unnumbered}

The public book begins with a theory-first foundation: commodity-market structure, storage and convenience yield, forward curves, futures and options valuation, stochastic price processes, econometrics, portfolio construction, and risk. Coding begins with deterministic fixtures and synthetic or redistributable data so that the accounting identities and statistical procedures can be audited before live data are introduced.

The Python framework grows alongside the theory. Agricultural contract, curve, fundamental, and portfolio objects belong in the domain layer. Generic stateful streaming operators, online statistics, and pipeline semantics can be contributed to Screamer when they are useful beyond agriculture; specialized agricultural logic remains in the domain layer.

Bloomberg connectivity, proprietary observations, and terminal-specific exercises are maintained in a separate private companion project. They will inform later applications, but the public book will not depend on Bloomberg access.

## How to study the book {.unnumbered}

Read the definitions and derivations before expanding the code. Treat every code cell as an executable specification of a market object or accounting identity. For each empirical result, ask what was observable at the decision time, what was estimated, what was tradable, what it cost, and which failure modes remain.

## Curriculum map {.unnumbered}

| Stage | Main question | Agricultural anchor |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1. Instruments and curves | What exactly is being traded, delivered, marked, and rolled? | CBOT corn contract months and calendar spreads |
| 2. Commodity economics and fundamentals | How do stocks, flows, weather, policy, and logistics enter prices? | WASDE balances, crop progress, basis, storage |
| 3. Statistical market research | Which signals survive timing controls, costs, regimes, and multiple testing? | Seasonality, curve carry, momentum, positioning, inter-commodity spreads |
| 4. Options and volatility | How are nonlinear exposures priced, hedged, and stress-tested? | Black-76, implied volatility, skew, report/event risk |
| 5. Portfolio construction and risk | How are heterogeneous trades combined under limits? | Futures, spreads, options, cross-commodity and cross-crop risk |
| 6. Research implementation | How does a hypothesis become a tested and monitored process? | Contract panels, public data, private adapters, attribution, model governance |

The first public module is intentionally narrow: it establishes the contract-level and forward-curve language on which the later theory, signals, options, and portfolio work depend.

## Current public scope {.unnumbered}

Module 1 contains the first contract-level lesson. Subsequent modules will add agricultural supply-demand balances, weather and crop information, basis, seasonality, stochastic models, options, portfolio construction, and risk. The selected reading and source map appears after the current modules and will evolve with the book.
